newsitem.title: USA: Dollar finishes lower in pre-weekend U.S. trade.
newsitem.headline: Dollar finishes lower in pre-weekend U.S. trade.

text.p: The U.S. currency ended lower amid uncertainty about Japan's currency policy and pre-weekend position-squaring, but late demand for dollars in the futures market helped erase most losses against the yen, experts said.

"Basically, a large buyer of dollar/yen came in the market and bought $170 million twice on the (International Monetary Market) in the last 40 minutes or so," said William Marr, manager of foreign exchange at Credit Commerciale de France.
The dollar had slid to an intraday low of 111.45 yen in New York, but bounced off the bottom to close at 111.70/75 yen, down marginally from 111.83/88 yen at the open.
The dollar finished at 1.5045/50 marks, down from 1.5107/10 marks at the open.

The dollar had declined sharply versus the yen on Thursday after a leading Japanese financial newspaper reported that Eisuke Sakakibara, director general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, said the Ministry was not trying to push the yen down further.

Market sentiment remained guarded on Friday even though Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told Reuters his government should not intervene in the currency markets and suggested Japan's interest rates would likely remain low.
Kevin Harris, an international economist at MCM CurrencyWatch, said the dollar slid versus the yen on concerns over Japanese foreign exchange policy.
"These policy changes are intentionally veiled," Harris said. "So, there's good reason to worry about this until we get a lot of clarification both from their statements and from their behavior."
The dollar was also briefly pressured after talk swept through the foreign exchange market on Friday that U.S. President Bill Clinton had been shot.
White House deputy press secretary Barry Toiv denied the rumor, saying the president was fine and at work in the Oval Office.

"There was a slight move downward on the dollar but it quickly dissipated," said Doug Lee, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Sakura Bank Ltd. "The denials came out very, very quickly."
Foreign exchange desks in the United States will be thinly staffed for the Veterans Day holiday on Monday. The Treasury bond market will also be closed, while the stock markets will remain open.
Curreny traders squared their books ahead of the holiday.
"I think they're nervous about having any kind of positions, just because the dollar has been making so many wild swings," said a trader at the New York branch of a major European bank.
Elsewhere, the dollar closed at 1.2640/50 Swiss francs, down from 1.2730/40 at the open.
The dollar inched up to C$1.3313/18 from C$1.3310/15. The Australian dollar closed at $0.7865/75, down from $0.7875/80 at the open. -- Donna Sells 212-859-1668
